# Writing copy

Load `unslop` and `plain-writing` first, then apply these six rules.

1. **No eyebrow lines.** Omit the small label or kicker above a heading or
   title unless the request asks for one.
2. **Question every piece of text.** Name the question it answers and whether
   anyone is really asking it. People usually are not. Cut it if not.
3. **Keep jargon out of explainers.** One word per idea, defined once. Reuse
   that word; do not cycle synonyms.
4. **One named audience.** Know who reads it before you write, and write for
   that person.
5. **No compliance narration.** Do not explain how an action follows a rule
   or why it does not break one, unless the reader asked or the action really
   sits on the rule's boundary; then state the decision in one clause and stop.
   Never explain a distinction the reader set up or plainly knows. After a
   correction, report what changed; do not reassure in later messages. The
   test: what would the reader misread without this sentence? If nothing, cut
   it.
6. **Three passes before sending.** Reread the whole draft three times, each
   pass with one question: is every claim correct; does every sentence answer
   something the reader is asking; is any sentence about the writer rather
   than the reader's subject (self-justification, reassurance, credit, effort).
   Take the most care with that last kind: it is the easiest to miss in your
   own writing. Fix and reread after each pass.

Subagents load `unslop` and `plain-writing` only when they write copy, or when
a reviewer fixes comments (build-loop A7).

# Boat

Boat (boat.dev) rents full Linux VMs ("sandboxes"): x86_64 Ubuntu, user
`user`, home `/home/user`, passwordless `sudo`, Docker and common toolchains,
billed per second while running. Older docs and third-party skills call it
**Box** (`box` CLI, `box.ascii.dev`, `on.ascii.dev`): same product, stale
names. Use `boat`. Inside a sandbox, agents get Boat's own `boat` skill; this
one is for driving sandboxes from here.

## Access

- The CLI is `boat` (on `PATH`; `~/.ascii/bin/boat`) and is already signed in:
  `boat status`. Never run `boat login`, `boat onboard` or an install script;
  if it says signed out, ask the user.
- A sandbox is reachable **only through the CLI** (`exec`, `ssh`, `scp`,
  `forward`). It is not on Tailscale and has no entry in `~/.ssh/config`.
- Always pass the explicit `bx_...` id. `current` and `self` do not work from
  a non-interactive shell here.
- Which sandbox: read `<project>.research/boat.md` (id, purpose, size, what
  secrets it holds). Update it when you create, trim or retire one.

## Commands

| Need | Command |
|---|---|
| State, size, TTL | `boat info <id>` (JSON; fields under `.sandbox`), `boat list` |
| Start / stop | `boat resume <id>`, `boat stop <id>` |
| Short command | `boat exec <id> --timeout 120 -- bash -lc '<cmd>'` (default timeout 30 s) |
| Long job | `boat exec <id> --detach -- bash -lc '<cmd> > ~/job.log 2>&1'` → prints `pid` |
| Wait for it | `boat exec <id> --attach <pid>` as a background Bash command (the harness notifies you); `--status <pid>`, `--kill <pid>` |
| Files | `boat scp ./f <id>:/home/user/f`, `boat scp <id>:/home/user/f ./f` |
| Source | `git bundle create x.bundle <branch>`, `scp` it, `git clone x.bundle` inside: no Git credentials enter the sandbox |
| Plan and hours | `boat limits`, `boat usage <id>`; never quote prices from memory |

`exec` prints one JSON line (`stdout`, `stderr`, exit code). Parse it, for
example `| python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.loads(sys.stdin.readline()); print(d["stdout"])'`.

## Gotchas seen here

- **Nix socket after resume.** The first Nix call after `resume` fails with
  "Permission denied" on the daemon socket. A plain restart can leave the
  socket at mode 0644, and a `chmod 666` alone later gives "Connection refused"
  once a detached job starts. What works (one `exec`): `sudo systemctl stop
  nix-daemon.service nix-daemon.socket; sudo rm -f
  /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket; sudo systemctl start nix-daemon.socket
  nix-daemon.service; sleep 3; sudo chmod 666
  /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket; nix store ping`. Then run detached jobs
  under `setpriv` (below). Source
  `/nix/var/nix/profiles/default/etc/profile.d/nix-daemon.sh` in each `exec`.
- **Capabilities.** `exec` processes carry ambient capabilities that break
  FHS/bubblewrap tools. Wrap detached runs:
  `--detach -- setpriv --ambient-caps -all --inh-caps -all bash -lc '...'`.
- **Nothing survives a stop** except the disk: relaunch services after
  `resume`. The IP changes on each resume.
- **Size.** Boat counts allocated disk; a sandbox past the default limit needs
  `--type large` to resume (2× cost). Trim or `nix-store --gc` instead of
  upsizing, and ask before choosing a paid size.
- **Memory.** Sandboxes have their own RAM (the qex queue is for this host),
  but default size is ~8 GB: one Gradle or emulator job at a time.

## Rules

- **Secrets stay put.** Never copy keys, tokens or signing keystores into a
  sandbox, and never print them, unless the user said so for that sandbox.
  `holdsCreatorLogins` in `info` shows whether account logins are on it; a
  sandbox made with `--no-env` has none.
- **Costs.** Stop a sandbox when the work is done. Create one only when the
  task needs it. Delete stopped sandboxes you created once nothing needs them,
  so they don't pile up. Sandboxes owned by another project or session are
  theirs: check (`boat exec <id> -- ps`) before touching one, and never stop
  one that is busy.

## Disk, starts and credit (owner, 2026-11-18)

- **40 GB cap.** When a sandbox's used disk passes 40 GB, start a fresh one
  from a small saved snapshot and stop the old one. Never save a snapshot over
  40 GB: a 49 GB saved snapshot stopped hydrating (stuck in phase `sysdelta`,
  even `echo` timed out), while a 3 GB one was ready in ~10 s. Keep saved
  snapshots to what runs need: toolchains and package caches, not build
  output, run directories or checkouts.
- **Starts.** New sandboxes use the daily start budget (`boat billing status`:
  `limits.starts.day`). While under 50% of it is used, start fresh sandboxes
  freely and don't spend effort cleaning inside them. From 50% on, reuse your
  sandboxes and clean inside them after each run (old run directories,
  finished build output, temp databases, logs already downloaded), harder past
  ~25 GB used. Always keep at least 50 starts in reserve for the day; reuse or
  wait rather than go below it.
- **Under 20 starts left (owner, 2026-11-21).** A stop-and-resume costs a start,
  so keep your own sandbox up a little longer than usual: let the idle TTL run
  out (or set `--ttl 3600`) instead of stopping right after a job, in case a
  fix or rebuild follows. Weigh that against hours: the credit pack is large
  (check `creditBalanceHours`), so hours are the cheaper thing to burn and
  starts the scarcer. Do not stretch it past the TTL, and still never leave one
  up overnight.
- **Name the sandbox (owner, 2026-11-22).** Project wrappers such as edge's
  `boat-run` have no default sandbox: pass `--sandbox ID` (or set
  `BOAT_SANDBOX`), or `--own`. They refuse other projects' sandboxes, and
  start a stopped one only with `--resume`, because each start uses a launch.
  Put the sandbox ID in every brief that runs Boat.
- **Size is not a saving (owner, 2026-11-21).** Do not hold back from `large`
  to save money. When a job needs the RAM, or a smaller size would force a
  resize (which costs a start), use `large`.
- **Credit after the plan runs out.** When the plan's included hours are used
  up, starts draw from the prepaid pack or wallet: check `creditBalanceHours`
  and `canStart` in `boat billing status` before calling Boat empty. Plan-hours
  counters alone undercount.
- **Sign-in.** `boat login` starts a new browser sign-in and signs the CLI out
  until it completes. Never run it from an agent; ask the user.

## Spend: cheap by default, fast under a deadline

Plan hours are finite (`boat limits`: `planIncluded.vmHoursRemaining`), a
`large` sandbox bills 2x, and a keepalive bills while nothing runs. Pick the
mode from the situation and say which one you are in.

| | Cheap (default) | Time crunch (owner deadline) |
|---|---|---|
| When | No deadline given | The owner asked for a result by a time |
| Size | `large` whenever the job needs the RAM or the sandbox is already `large`; `default` only for light test iterations on a sandbox that is already `default` | `large` throughout |
| Idle | Sandbox stops itself ~15 min after the last job (`boat-run` and `boat-sync-test` set the idle TTL); stop it explicitly at the end of a batch | Keep it up for the window; still stop it when the deadline work is delivered |
| Runs | Targeted files; batch checks into one run; full suite only at a gate (before pushing a shared branch) | Same targeting; run independent jobs in parallel; start a warm build early |
| Never | Leave a sandbox up overnight, or a 2-hour keepalive for one quick run | Run past the deadline work at `large` "while you are there" |

Check the spend once a session (`boat limits`, `boat usage <id>`) and say it
when the remaining hours will not reach the plan's period end at the current
rate. Shrinking (`boat resume <id> --type default`) needs the data to fit:
trim old run directories and `nix-store --gc` first.
- **Docs.** `https://docs.boat.dev/llms.txt` lists every page; fetch any page
  as `.md`. `boat <command> --help` is authoritative for flags.

# Unslop

**Exception (owner, 2026-11-20): Gemini Neon does not load this skill.** Its copy is trialled
without it; the owner will revisit the decision after the trial. Every other model still follows it.

Edit text to remove AI patterns and add human voice.

## Process

1. Scan for the patterns below.
2. Rewrite. Preserve meaning, match intended tone.
3. Add soul (see next section).
4. Self-audit: "What makes this obviously AI generated?" Fix remaining tells.

## Adding soul

Removing patterns is half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious.

- **Have opinions.** React to facts instead of neutrally listing pros and cons.
- **Vary rhythm.** Short sentences. Then longer ones that take their time. Mix it up.
- **Acknowledge complexity.** "Impressive but also kind of unsettling" beats "impressive."
- **Use "I" when it fits.** First person isn't unprofessional.
- **Let some mess in.** Perfect structure looks machine-made.
- **Be specific.** Not "this is concerning" but "there's something unsettling about agents churning away at 3am."

## Summary first

The opening of a reply carries everything the reader must know or could be misled
by, not only the result (owner, 2026-11-21). A caveat that first appears in the
last paragraph is a failure, even if the detail repeats it higher up. Before
sending, ask what the owner would be annoyed to learn only from the end, and move
it into the opening summary as one plain sentence:

- Anything not verified: not run on a device, delivery sent but unconfirmed,
  tests skipped, assumed rather than observed.
- A result that differs from the ask: a deviation from the mock-up, a switch left
  off, a default you chose for them.
- Risks and one-way steps: an install that can fail, data that could be lost,
  money spent, a build left running.
- Decisions you made for them, and what you could not decide.

Lead with these, then give the detail below. Repeating a caveat later is fine.

## Patterns to detect and fix

### Content

1. **Puffery.** "pivotal moment", "testament to", "evolving landscape", "setting the stage for", "indelible mark", "deeply rooted". Cut puffery, state what happened.
2. **Name-dropping.** Listing media outlets without context. Pick one, say what was said.
3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
4. **Promotional language.** "nestled", "vibrant", "breathtaking", "groundbreaking", "renowned", "stunning", "must-visit". Use neutral descriptions.
5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
6. **Formulaic challenges.** "Despite challenges... continues to thrive." Replace with specific facts.

### Language

7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Just say "is" or "has".
9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
10. **Unsupported contrasts.** Do not rebut a diagnosis the reader has not made. Remove phrases such as "not X," "rather than X," "as opposed to X," or "this isn't X" unless X was explicitly claimed earlier. Even when a comparison is useful or requested, state the positive evidence and evaluation path instead of negating X. Ask: "Who claimed X?" If the answer is nobody, state the supported fact directly.
11. **Rule of three.** Forcing ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
12. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
13. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.

### Style

13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). Em dashes are an AI tell, and reaching for parentheses instead just trades one tell for another. If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example. Not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
19. **Curly quotes.** Replace with straight quotes.

### Communication artifacts

20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
21. **Cutoff disclaimers.** "While specific details are limited..." Find sources or remove.
22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
32. **Buried caveats.** Unverified claims, deviations from the ask, risks and decisions made for the owner appear only in the last paragraph or only inside a detail list. Move them into the opening summary (see "Summary first").

### Filler

23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". "It is important to note that" gets deleted.
24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.

### Jargon

26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate, wedge, vector, locus, vantage, nexus, primitive (as noun), harness (as metaphor), surface (as in "API surface"), bedrock, scaffolding (as metaphor), modality, paradigm, gold-plating, ratchet (as metaphor), evacuate (for moving code), endgame, north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. "Substrate" becomes "base". "Wedge in" becomes "add". "Vector" becomes "way" or "method". "Gold-plating" becomes "more than the job needs". "Ratchet" becomes the mechanism's real name or "a limit that only tightens". "Evacuate" becomes "move out". "Endgame" becomes "the last phase". Pick the concrete word.

### Plain speech

27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number. "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" becomes "use", "leverage" becomes "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.

# Plain writing

Write plain and direct. Apply from the first sentence, to your own replies and
summaries as much as to drafts you're handed.

## Three vices to cut

**1. Deep jargon.** An acronym or insider term used without defining it, or
several undefined terms stacked in one sentence. Define each term in a few plain
words on first use, or don't use it. Covers corporate shorthand, not just
technical terms.
- No: "We'll leverage the Q3 GTM motion to move the needle on NRR."
- Yes: "In the third quarter we'll aim the sales plan at getting current
  customers to spend more."
- Reuse the short form after one definition: "annual recurring revenue (ARR) —
  the subscription income we count on each year" then "ARR."

**2. Throat-clearing.** Preamble and narration about what the text is about to
do. Don't announce structure, editorialize your reasoning, or warm up. Cut "it's
worth being concrete," "before we get into it," "the honest truth is," "this is
the part that matters most."
- No: "Before the details, it's worth stepping back. The honest truth is
  onboarding is broken."
- Yes: "Onboarding is broken: four in ten new users quit before finishing setup."
- Cousin — claiming a virtue instead of showing it: "the honest answer," "to be
  fair," "frankly," "the real question." Delete the label, keep the sentence.

**3. Showing off.** Flourish that sounds clever instead of informing. No
rhetorical triads, aphorisms, italics for drama, cute headings, or punchline
sentences. Cut any sentence doing rhetorical work rather than carrying
information.
- No: "We shipped fast, we shipped hard, and we shipped it *beautiful*."
- Yes: "We shipped the redesign in six weeks."
- Also cut the stacked "not X; Y" antithesis and the punchy fragment for emphasis
  ("Users absorb that as normal. It isn't.").

## Two positive rules

- Plain words, active voice, one idea per sentence in the opening.
- Readable, not dry: lead with a concrete example and keep the prose flowing.

## Mechanics

- Active voice: "The team missed the deadline," not "was missed by the team."
  Passive only when the actor is unknown or irrelevant.
- Present tense for what a thing does: "This setting hides the sidebar."
- Address the reader as "you." "We" only for shared work you're part of.
- Condition before instruction: "If payment fails, retry once."
- One idea per sentence: split on a second "and" or a load-bearing "which."
- Define a term on first use: long form, short form in parentheses, then short
  form.
- Cut reader-blaming softeners: "simply," "just," "easy," "obviously," "of
  course."
- Cut filler openers: "It's worth noting that," "Basically," "At the end of the
  day."
- Sentence case for headings.
- Unambiguous dates: "2026-08-20" or "August 20, 2026," never "08/09."
- Technical writing: code, commands, filenames, and literals in monospace; UI
  names in bold.

## Cutting length

Revision bloats through repetition: a reframing gets patched into every section,
and one claim ends up stated five ways. Reading straight through won't catch it;
counting will.
- List the distinct claims (assertions, not sections); find and count each. Give
  a repeated claim one home — where the argument is developed, not previewed. A
  summary restating a developed claim is fine; the same argument at full strength
  twice is not.
- Sweep for dangling references — ordinals, comparatives, coined shorthand whose
  antecedent was cut. Name what each points at; if you can't, it dangles.
- When cuts run out and it's still too long, don't promise a length you can't
  hit. Say early: "hitting that length means dropping an argument — here are the
  candidates; which do you want to lose?"

## Structure is a separate pass

These rules fix prose, not structure. A malformed header, a claim ordered before
its setup, a section that overpromises — each fails independently. State the
format's fixed requirements explicitly and run its check or template. Only a
check guarantees structure.

## Reusable prompt block

Prepend when prompting a model to draft prose:

```text
Write this in a plain, direct voice. Follow these rules strictly:
1. No undefined jargon. Define any acronym or insider term in a few plain words on first use, or don't use it. Never stack several undefined terms in one sentence.
2. No throat-clearing. Don't announce what you're about to do, don't narrate structure, don't editorialize your reasoning. State the thing.
3. No showing off. No rhetorical triads, aphorisms, italics for drama, cute headings, or lines that exist to sound clever. Cut any sentence doing rhetorical work rather than carrying information.
4. Plain words, active voice, one idea per sentence in the opening.
5. Still readable — not choppy or dry. Lead with a concrete example and keep the prose flowing.
```

## Self-check

- Any acronym or specialist term undefined on first use?
- Any sentence announcing what you're about to do instead of doing it?
- Any line there to sound clever rather than inform?
- Gentle to read, or a list of assertions?

If the project or publication has a style guide, it wins where they disagree.

## Provenance

Distilled from [evanphx/llm-voice](https://github.com/evanphx/llm-voice): a
15-model study of how voice directives change model-written prose. Complements
the `unslop` skill (pattern removal) — plain-writing targets structural voice
rules (jargon, preamble, performative prose). See also
`knowledge/tools/llm-voice.md`.

104	 * Settings as top tabs: Features, Notifications, Apps, Focus, More. Inside a tab there is at most one level more:
105	 * the sound-control pages and a single app's page open over the tabs, and the schedule editor, backup, about and
106	 * the focus tools' own screens are pushed routes.
107	 */
108	@Composable
109	internal fun SettingsScreen(
110	    selectedTab: SettingsTab,
111	    onSelectTab: (SettingsTab) -> Unit,
112	    state: MainScreenState,
113	    onEvent: (MainScreenEvent) -> Unit,
114	    switches: FeatureSwitches,
115	    onUsageChange: (Boolean) -> Unit,
116	    onLauncherChange: (Boolean) -> Unit,
117	    onFocusChange: (Boolean) -> Unit,
118	    snackbarHostState: SnackbarHostState,
119	    isDarkMode: Boolean,
120	    shouldShowRational: (String) -> Boolean,
121	    onOpen: (String) -> Unit,
122	) {
123	    // The app's package name, not a SettingsSubPage, so it survives rotation and process death.
124	    var appPackage by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf<String?>(null) }
125	    var soundOpen by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }
126	    // Switching tab, including through the Inbox gear, drops an app page or sound page left open on another tab.
127	    androidx.compose.runtime.LaunchedEffect(selectedTab) { appPackage = null; soundOpen = false }
128	    val subPage: SettingsSubPage? = when {
129	        soundOpen -> SettingsSubPage.Sound
130	        appPackage != null -> SettingsSubPage.App(appPackage!!)
131	        else -> null
132	    }
133	    BackHandler(enabled = subPage != null) {
134	        if (soundOpen) soundOpen = false else appPackage = null
135	    }
136	
137	    Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
138	        Column(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
139	            CommonAppBar(title = stringResource(R.string.settings), onNavigateUp = null)
140	            SettingsTabRow(selectedTab, onSelectTab)
141	            when (selectedTab) {
142	                SettingsTab.Features -> FeaturesTab(
143	                    state, onEvent, switches, onUsageChange, onLauncherChange, onFocusChange, onOpen,
144	                )
145	                SettingsTab.Notifications -> NotificationSettingsPage(
146	                    shouldShowRational = shouldShowRational,
147	                    snackbarHostState = snackbarHostState,
148	                    isDarkMode = isDarkMode,
149	                    onOpenSchedule = { onOpen(Routes.NOTIFICATION_SCHEDULE_EDITOR) },
150	                    onOpenSound = { soundOpen = true },
151	                )
152	                // The list stays composed under an app's page, so Back returns to the same search and scroll.
153	                SettingsTab.Apps -> AppPriorityScreen(onOpenApp = { appPackage = it })
154	                SettingsTab.Focus -> FocusSettingsTab(onOpen)
155	                SettingsTab.More -> MoreTab(state, onEvent, onOpen)
156	            }
157	        }
158	        when (val page = subPage) {
159	            null -> Unit
160	            SettingsSubPage.Sound -> SubPageSurface {
161	                NotificationSoundControlPage(onBack = { soundOpen = false })
162	            }
163	            is SettingsSubPage.App -> SubPageSurface {
164	                CommonAppBar(title = stringResource(R.string.settings_tab_apps), onNavigateUp = { appPackage = null })
165	                AppPriorityDetail(page.packageName) { AppFocusSection(page.packageName) }
166	            }
167	        }
168	    }
169	}

Farhan: Your Smart, Distraction-Free Companion in the Android World.

Farhan is an open-source and powerful Android application that empowers you to take control of your digital experience. Included features:

  1. Notifications Filter: Tired of constant interruptions? The Notifications Filter in Farhan puts you back in control of your notifications. The app intelligently filters notifications, ensuring you stay centered without missing any important alerts. You can also exclude specific apps from the filter, ensuring important notifications reach you. Plus, easily access filtered notifications directly from within the app.

  4. Usage Check: Get a comprehensive overview of your app usage patterns with the Usage Check feature in Farhan. The simple interface makes it easy to understand and manage your usage data.

/** The two accesses Android grants through its own screens. Both are read, never changed, from Settings. */
internal data class SystemAccessChecks(
    val notificationAccess: Boolean = false,
    val accessibility: Boolean = false,
)

@HiltViewModel
internal class SpecialAccessChecksViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val serviceUtil: ServiceUtil,
    private val grayscale: GrayscaleUseCases,
) : ViewModel() {
    var checks by mutableStateOf(SystemAccessChecks())
        private set

            val next = SystemAccessChecks(
                notificationAccess = serviceUtil.isNotificationAccessPermissionGranted(),
                accessibility = grayscale.isAccessibilityPermissionGranted(),
            )
            if (next != checks) checks = next
        }
    }
}

- **Rotation:** the open flow page and its route survive rotation and split-screen resize. A run in flight and a shown result do not. The pairing code is held only in composition and cleared on submit.
- **Result timing:** the controller reads each connector result once, then calls `dismissResult()`. A result arriving while Settings is not composed is shown when you return.

**Deviations from v5**
- **Notification access and Accessibility rows:** real checks exist (`ServiceUtil.isNotificationAccessPermissionGranted`, `GrayscaleUseCases.isAccessibilityPermissionGranted`), so both rows show. They show "Not allowed" when off, which the mock never does.

- **Red note:** hidden when sensitive notifications are allowed or not applicable (before Android 15). It no longer depends on the "hidden" flag alone.
